query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A machine learning–based interatomic potential, trained on DFT data for both the solid and liquid phases near melting, can enable efficient two-phase coexistence or interface pinning simulations to accurately predict the melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, matching DFT-level results with significantly reduced computational cost.
generation.material_initial_state: High-melting refractory material in its solid phase near the melting point (with coexisting solid and liquid regions accessible via simulation).
generation.intervention: Replace the expensive ab initio thermodynamic integration process with simulations using a DFT-trained machine learning interatomic potential.
generation.conditions: Simulations conducted near the melting temperature under the high-temperature regime using efficient two-phase coexistence or interface pinning methods to sample both solid and liquid phases.
generation.structural_mediator: A machine learning interatomic potential that accurately captures the interatomic interactions for both phases.
generation.mechanism: By training the ML model on DFT-calculated energies and forces, the method retains near ab initio accuracy. Subsequent high-throughput simulations of phase coexistence (or interface pinning) allow for efficient extraction of melting properties, thereby bypassing the high computational cost of full thermodynamic integration.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML-based simulation framework will predict melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change within error margins comparable to DFT-based predictions, but at a fraction of the computational cost.
generation.baseline: Conventional ab initio free-energy approaches using thermodynamic integration with ab initio molecular dynamics, which are highly accurate but computationally prohibitive for high-throughput studies.
generation.boundary: Accuracy is contingent upon the quality and transferability of the ML potential; for conditions significantly outside the training regime (e.g., extreme pressures or compositions), the predictions may deviate from DFT benchmarks.
generation.uncertainty: The degree to which the ML potential can generalize to all relevant high-temperature phase configurations remains uncertain and may require further validation against experimental or full DFT simulation data.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop a machine learning interatomic potential using DFT training data for both the solid and liquid phases near melting. Use this potential to perform two-phase coexistence (or interface pinning) molecular dynamics simulations to compute the melting temperature, latent heat (enthalpy of fusion), entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting. Validate these computed melting properties by comparing them to a subset of full DFT-based thermodynamic integration results and available experimental data.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the melting properties predicted by the ML-driven simulation deviate significantly (beyond an acceptable error margin, e.g., greater than 5-10% difference) from DFT reference calculations or experimental observations, then the hypothesis that the ML potential can accurately replace expensive ab initio methods for these properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Machine-learning interatomic potential

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems [24] , [44] – [46] . Here, using training data reported previously [24] for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost [46] . The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1 . decision.trend: Early works using DFT‐based free‐energy calculations achieved high accuracy for phase-transition properties via thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamics, but these methods are extremely costly. Over time, researchers have begun to use data‐driven approaches – for example, machine learning interatomic potentials – to accelerate high‐temperature simulations. One notable example (PMC8357793) demonstrated that ML potentials can capture key high-T phenomena (e.g., dislocation mobility) at nearly ab initio accuracy with far less computational expense. However, while these ML methods have been applied to study mechanical or defect properties, the integration of such techniques to predict complete melting properties (melting temperature, latent heats, and volume changes) remains largely unexplored.
decision.unsolved: There is currently no method that combines DFT-level accuracy with computational efficiency for high-throughput calculation of all melting properties. Key challenges include achieving robust sampling of both solid and liquid phases near the melting point without the prohibitive cost associated with full thermodynamic integration.
decision.lever: Develop a machine learning-based interatomic potential trained on DFT data for both the solid and liquid phases near melting. Then apply an efficient two-phase coexistence or interface pinning method using this ML model to extract melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, and volume change at melting.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of leveraging ML potentials to bypass the high computational cost of direct ab initio MD while retaining near DFT-level accuracy. It directly addresses the gap by enabling high-throughput, accurate predictions of complete melting properties in high-melting refractory materials.
